zebralogic.title: Enforce uniqueness across each attribute category
zebralogic.principle: Each value in a category must appear exactly once across all houses; duplicate assignments violate the puzzle constraints.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When assigning values to houses, check that each attribute value is used only once within its category.
zebralogic.example: Assigning the same mother name to two different houses.

zebralogic.title: Preserve original case of attribute values
zebralogic.principle: Copy attribute values verbatim as they appear in the problem statement, preserving spelling and case.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When constructing the final JSON output, use the exact strings from the puzzle.

zebralogic.title: Bidirectional equivalence for name‑attribute clues
zebralogic.principle: If a clue links a specific name to an attribute, enforce both directions: the name must have that attribute and that attribute must belong to that name.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue says something like "The person whose mother's name is Sarah is the person who prefers city breaks" or any name‑to‑attribute link.
zebralogic.example: Only enforcing Name→Mother but not Mother→Name, allowing the mother to be assigned elsewhere.

zebralogic.title: Bidirectional equivalence for attribute‑attribute clues
zebralogic.principle: When a clue states that two non‑name attributes belong to the same house, enforce that they co‑occur in both directions.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue says something like "The person who likes going on cruises has a child named Meredith".
zebralogic.example: Linking Vacation=cruise to Child=Meredith but not also linking Child=Meredith back to Vacation=cruise.

zebralogic.title: Apply direct placement constraints
zebralogic.principle: If a clue explicitly places an attribute in a specific house number, enforce that placement and propagate any linked attributes.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue says something like "The person who loves fantasy books is in the third house".
zebralogic.example: Placing fantasy at house 3 but forgetting to also place the linked name Carol there.

zebralogic.title: Output solution JSON with exact schema and no extra text
zebralogic.principle: Emit only the JSON object with top‑level keys 'reasoning' and 'solution' and the required table; any extra text causes parsing errors.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: At the very end of the response, after all reasoning.
zebralogic.example: Adding a concluding sentence after the JSON object.

zebralogic.title: Chain adjacency clues into consecutive blocks
zebralogic.principle: When multiple adjacency clues share a common intermediate attribute, treat them as a chain to form a consecutive block of houses.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When clues like "A is directly left of B" and "B is directly left of C" appear.
zebralogic.example: Placing A left of B and B left of C but not ensuring they occupy three consecutive houses.

zebralogic.title: Interpret ordering and adjacency clues correctly (including N houses between)
zebralogic.principle: Parse directional terms ('left of', 'right of', 'next to') and distance clues ('two houses between') accurately, respecting both direction and exact spacing.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: Whenever a clue involves relative positions of houses.
zebralogic.example: Treating 'two houses between' as a distance of two instead of requiring three positions apart.

zebralogic.title: Chain equivalence clues across multiple attributes
zebralogic.principle: If multiple clues each link a pair of attributes, combine them transitively so that all linked attributes co‑occur in the same house.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When equivalence clues form a chain, e.g., A↔B, B↔C, C↔D.
zebralogic.example: Linking Mother=Kailyn↔Vacation=cruise, Vacation=cruise↔Child=Meredith, but not also linking Child=Meredith↔Mother=Kailyn.

zebralogic.title: Disambiguate bare name references in ordering clues
zebralogic.principle: When a clue mentions a name without an explicit attribute qualifier, interpret it as referring to the Name attribute (the adult), not to other categories like Child or Mother, even if that name also appears as a possible value in those categories.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: In ordering, adjacency, or placement clues that contain a plain name (e.g., "Alice") without a qualifier.
zebralogic.example: Interpreting "The child's name Bella is somewhere to the left of Alice" as Bella left of the child named Alice instead of the person named Alice.

zebralogic.description: Interpreting 'N houses between' as distance N
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model confuses the phrase 'between' with a simple offset, forgetting that 'two houses between' means a gap of three positions.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Count the houses that lie strictly between the two referenced houses; the positional difference should be N+1.

zebralogic.description: Ignoring equivalence clues that bind two attributes to the same house
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model treats each clue in isolation and does not propagate linked attributes across clues.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: When a clue states A ↔ B, record a bidirectional link and ensure A and B are assigned together in the same house.

zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model does not keep a global record of used values for each attribute category.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Maintain a set of used values for each category and forbid repeats when assigning new values.

zebralogic.description: Altering attribute values (spelling/casing) instead of copying them verbatim
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model normalizes text or assumes case‑insensitivity, changing the original strings.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Copy attribute strings exactly as they appear in the puzzle statement, preserving case and spelling.

zebralogic.description: Including extra explanatory text or stray characters outside the required JSON solution
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model adds a concluding remark or extra formatting after the JSON object.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Output only the JSON object with the required top‑level keys and nothing else.
